walkthroughs.body_html:
International Trade and the Global Economy — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

International Trade and the Global Economy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with International Trade and the Global Economy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Specialisation based on lowest opportunity cost is:
options: Absolute advantage
Comparative advantage
Free trade
Protectionism

mcqs.q: A tariff is a tax on:
options: Exports
Imports
Domestic production
Consumption

mcqs.q: What did the original Phillips curve suggest, and how has thinking changed?
options: The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
Real GDP is GDP only from physical goods; nominal GDP includes services.
The Phillips curve still proves you can always reduce unemployment by allowing more inflation.

The original Phillips curve suggested a stable inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Friedman and the 1970s stagflation experience added expectations — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

mcqs.q: How does raising interest rates reduce inflation?
options: The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing consumption and investment — lowering aggregate demand and slowing price rises.
Higher interest rates directly force shops to lower their prices.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between real GDP, nominal GDP and GNI?
options: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP adjusts for inflation; GNI (Gross National Income) is GDP plus net income from abroad (similar to old GNP). Each answers a different question about economic activity.
Real GDP is GDP only from physical goods; nominal GDP includes services.
Real GDP, nominal GDP and GNI are interchangeable terms.
The Phillips curve shows the link between phone use and unemployment.
